content.title: About
content.content: Cheese, Mexican blend (540) is a semi‑hard cheese infused with the bold flavors of chili, paprika and other spices typical of Mexican cuisine. Made from cow’s milk, it has a slightly spicy bite and a golden‑orange hue derived from natural seasonings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese is commonly used in tacos, burritos and fajitas to add a distinctive aroma.
Traditional recipes include smoked chilies, cumin and garlic, giving it a rich flavor profile.
It is especially popular in U.S. regions with strong Mexican food demand, such as Texas and California.
The cheese can be sliced thinly or grated, making it versatile for cooking.
Sodium content is usually higher than in plain cheeses because of the added spices.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Provides high‑quality milk protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Rich in calcium and phosphorus, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic cultures
items.content: Some versions are produced with live cultures that may benefit gut health.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Contains monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Lactose content may cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Added spices increase sodium levels; people with hypertension should limit portions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese is energy‑dense; excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mexican blend cheese works well as a topping for tacos, burritos, casseroles, and as a flavorful addition to salads and soups. It can be sliced, grated, or melted into sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cheese in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage (over 2‑3 weeks) it can be frozen after portioning. Discard if mold, off‑odor, or slimy texture appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Oysters are marine bivalve mollusks that live in coastal waters. Steaming preserves their natural briny flavor, tender texture, and most of their nutrients. They are often served hot, drizzled with sauce or lemon.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: An oyster can filter up to 50 liters of water per day, helping to clean its environment.
They have been considered a delicacy for more than 3,000 years, mentioned in ancient Chinese and Roman texts.
Oysters contain more zinc per serving than any other food.
They can change sex depending on environmental conditions.
In Japan, the tradition of “omakase” lets diners choose oysters without knowing the exact variety.

items.title: Rich in zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function, wound healing, and reproductive health.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Steamed oysters provide few calories while delivering protein and minerals.

items.title: Contains omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s promote heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: The protein in oysters is easily digestible and supports muscle growth.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to oysters.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Oysters can accumulate toxins and bacteria, so purchase them from reputable sources.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: While modest, the cholesterol in oysters should be considered by those with high cholesterol.

items.title: Raw food safety
items.content: Steamed oysters may still harbor live microbes; ensure they are fully heated through.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve steamed oysters hot, often with lemon, soy sauce, or a butter‑based sauce. They can be eaten directly from the shell using a fork, or the meat can be removed and added to soups, pastas, or salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep live oysters in the refrigerator on a bed of damp cloth, no more than 2 days. Cooked oysters should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 24 hours.

shellfish-and-noodles-with-tomato-based-.title: Shellfish and noodles with tomato-based sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish combines fresh shellfish (usually mussels), al dente noodles, and a tomato‑based sauce seasoned with garlic, basil, and olive oil. Shellfish provide high‑quality protein and minerals, while the noodles supply complex carbohydrates, and the tomato sauce adds vitamin C and lycopene.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shellfish are one of the fastest‑growing seafoods; they can be fully cooked in 3–5 minutes.
Cooked tomatoes increase the bioavailability of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
The tradition of pairing seafood with pasta originated in Mediterranean cuisine, where sea flavors often meet tomato sauces.
Durum‑wheat noodles retain their shape in thick sauces, keeping the dish "al dente".
Shellfish are a rare non‑plant source of vitamin B12, essential for nerve health.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shellfish contain high‑quality marine protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Mineral source
items.content: Mussels are abundant in zinc, iron, and selenium, which aid immune function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Lycopene in the sauce
items.content: Thermally processed tomatoes boost lycopene absorption, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with moderate olive oil, the dish remains low in saturated fats.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids in shellfish help lower triglycerides and improve vascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shellfish.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Shellfish can accumulate toxins and heavy metals; purchase from reputable suppliers.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: Large portions of shellfish may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, tossing the noodles with the sauce and shellfish. Garnish with fresh basil, grated Parmesan, or a pinch of red pepper flakes for extra heat. A wide plate helps retain the aromatic sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh shellfish in a sealed container in the refrigerator for 1‑2 days. Cooked noodles and sauce can be stored separately in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Bean soup with meat is a hearty dish made from cooked beans, chunks of beef or pork, and aromatic vegetables. It is popular in many cuisines where beans provide protein and meat adds a rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, grown for over 7,000 years.
A traditional Russian version is called “bean soup with meat” and is often served in cold weather.
Some regions add smoked sausage to enhance a smoky aroma.
Bean soup is frequently used as a base for more complex dishes such as chili.
Legumes, including beans, can fix nitrogen in the soil, improving its fertility.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans contain about 20 % protein, making them a good source of amino acids, especially when combined with meat.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Both beans and meat are high in iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup provides vitamin B6, niacin, and folate, supporting energy metabolism and the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies magnesium, potassium, and phosphorus, important for muscle and bone health.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using prepared broth or adding salt can raise sodium levels, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Beans contain oligosaccharides that can cause gas and bloating in sensitive people.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Low‑quality or undercooked meat may harbor pathogens; ensure it is cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often with a slice of bread or croutons. It keeps well in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days and can be reheated. For extra flavor add fresh herbs, sour cream, or a dash of hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup quickly and store it in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed chitterlings are a traditional Puerto Rican dish consisting of slowly simmered pork intestines flavored with garlic, oregano, vinegar, olive oil, and aromatic spices such as adobo and cumin. The dish is often served with rice, beans, and plantains, and appears as a festive appetizer at family gatherings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chitterlings have been prepared in Puerto Rico for over 300 years.
Traditional preparation includes a pre‑soak in vinegar to remove odor.
The dish is commonly cooked in a "parrilló," a clay pot that retains moisture and flavor.
In Puerto Rican culture, chitterlings symbolize frugality and nose‑to‑tail cooking.
A sweet‑potato version exists, adding a subtle sweetness to the stew.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork intestines provide a rich source of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Good source of iron
items.content: Iron in chitterlings helps maintain hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system health and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish fits well into low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugar.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Pork intestines can harbor harmful bacteria; thorough cooking to safe internal temperature is essential.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Chitterlings are cholesterol‑rich, so people with heart disease should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to pork proteins.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Elevated purines can exacerbate gout symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve stewed chitterlings hot, typically alongside rice, beans, fried plantains, or mashed potatoes. They can be sliced and added to stews, tacos, or used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chitterlings in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) is a semi-aquatic plant in the cabbage family that grows in flowing water. It has small dark green leaves, tender stems, and a sharp peppery flavor. Watercress is eaten fresh in salads, sandwiches, and smoothies and added to soups, sauces, and appetizers. It is different from garden cress.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Watercress is one of the oldest edible leafy greens.
It is related to mustard, radish, cabbage, and wasabi.
It grows in flowing water, such as streams and special beds.
The sharp peppery flavor is created by glucosinolates, which turn into isothiocyanates.
In the United Kingdom, watercress is a traditional ingredient of soups and tea sandwiches.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K plays a role in blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains vitamin A
items.content: The body can partly convert the carotenoids in the leaves into vitamin A.

items.title: Contains isothiocyanates
items.content: These compounds, as in other cruciferous vegetables, are studied as antioxidants.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Watercress is very low in calories and adds a bright flavor.

items.title: Vitamin K and blood thinners
items.content: People taking warfarin and other anticoagulants should not suddenly change how much of these foods they eat without consulting a doctor.

items.title: Wild cress
items.content: Watercress collected in the wild may be contaminated with parasites such as liver fluke, and with bacteria; it is safer to buy cress grown in clean water.

items.title: Thyroid
items.content: A large amount of raw cruciferous vegetables may affect the thyroid in people with iodine deficiency.

items.title: Pungency
items.content: The sharp taste can irritate a sensitive stomach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wash watercress thoroughly and eat it fresh in salads, sandwiches, and smoothies, or add it to soups, omelets, sauces, and pesto. It is best added at the end of cooking to keep its pungency and color. Tough stems can be removed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh cress is very delicate: stand the stems in a glass of water in the refrigerator, covered with a bag, or wrap them in a damp paper towel. Use within two to three days.
